newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's new exchange chief to tighten up bourse.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's new exchange chief to tighten up bourse.

text.p: Amman's stock exchange chief-in-waiting said on Thursday he would push for tighter market accountability and efficiency to draw foreign investment and widen public share ownership in Jordan.
Wahib Shair, whose appointment as Director-General of Amman Financial Markets was approved by Jordan's cabinet this week, said the exchange needed greater transparency to lure international finance.
"We need to bring in the support of world investors and we need to prove we are clean and competitive," he told Reuters.
Shair, senior national partner at Allied Accountants, a member firm of Arthur Andersen and Co, takes over on October 15. He replaces Umayya Toukan who has run the exchange since November 1991.

Shair said he supported Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti's aim of widening public share ownership and would press for the government to pass a draft securities law aimed at making the market more attractive to international funds.
"The world wants commitment to efficiency...We want to improve corporate governance, to reduce the risk of corporate failure or corruption," Shair said.
He said he hoped to build on a cross-listing agreement with Bahrain to expand links with other Middle East exchanges.

The Amman exchange, already suffering from high domestic interest rates, was further hit this year by the stalled Middle East peace process and the delay in implementing a limited oil-for-food deal with Jordan's biggest trading partner Iraq.
Market capitalisation fell nine percent to 2.9 billion dinars ($4.1 billion) at the end of July from 3.2 billion at the start of the year.
But brokers say authorities have compounded market woes by piling new issues onto an already fragile exchange, weakening prices on a cash-strapped maarket.
Some brokers gave a cautious welcome to Shair's appointment.
"He's laid out the right priorities but he must keep in close touch with the brokers on the exchange," said one broker who asked not to be named. "Toukan lived in an ivory tower."
